selected.name: Transgressive Integration
selected.instruction: Score 10 when taboo or shocking material is integrated into a specific reversal, image, or narrative mechanism; score 0 when shock value is the entire joke.
selected.rationale: R25 and R56 use highly transgressive premises whose quality depends on whether the taboo element does more than provoke.
member_names: Blunt partisan/taboo claim, no comic cushioning
Bodily or sexual taboo as comic engine
Transgression carried by construction, not by a shock token

selected.name: Self-contained text; no link dependency or off-topic tags
selected.instruction: Score whether the joke is fully delivered by the visible words, with no reliance on an attached URL, image, or extra hashtags, and no tag clutter beyond the contest hashtag and the host handle. 10 = every element of the humor is recoverable from the text alone and nothing beyond the contest hashtag and host handle is present. 5 = self-contained but carrying one stray extra hashtag or redundant tag. 0 = the line is a caption or setup whose payload evidently sits in a linked image or video, or is buried under additional unrelated hashtags that narrow the audience to a subgroup. Score the dependency, not the topic.
selected.rationale: The three lowest dense percentiles in the whole slice are exactly the three link-bearing rows: R44 (0.010, 'automotive lawn art' plus a URL), R26 (0.022, 'David Brent in porn flick' plus a URL), R05 (0.049, 'I saw myself on @midnight' plus a URL), and all three are mid-to-high on the card. Rows carrying extra hashtags behave the same way: R23 ('#PointsMe #July4thBirthday', dense 0.042 / card 0.554) and R30 ('#STLCards', dense 0.223 / card 0.926). A criterion bank reading the visible words for wit will happily score these; a reader of the whole item sees an empty or fenced-off line.
member_names: Focus undiluted by self-promo or meta reference
Punchline-terminal delivery; tags do not interrupt
Self-contained text; no link dependency or off-topic tags

selected.name: Narrative Escalation
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an ordinary premise sharply escalates into a disproportionate or unsettling endpoint; score 0 when there is no progression or surprise.
selected.rationale: R18 escalates an accident into an embarrassing bodily consequence, and R47 turns a routine visit into an enduring threat.

selected.name: Morphological Wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a coined, blended, or altered word creates an immediate layered joke; score 0 when the wording contains no meaningful linguistic transformation.
selected.rationale: R07 and R39 build compact jokes from uncledad and bruncle, showing word formation doing more work than ordinary phrases.

selected.name: Concrete Cultural Texture
selected.instruction: Score 10 when specific objects, places, or practices create a vivid, culturally grounded world; score 0 when the entry relies only on vague labels.
selected.rationale: R04 evokes a particular rural place, and R58 uses a tightly selected set of concrete regional details.

selected.name: Surface-Meaning Irony
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the literal wording clearly conflicts with an implied comic meaning; score 0 when the statement is straightforward and has no interpretive reversal.
selected.rationale: R08 and R37 use affirmative or grammatical surfaces to suggest doubt about America, creating a meaningful gap between wording and implication.

selected.name: Alliteration, rhyme, or rhythmic sound-play
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet uses clear alliteration, internal rhyme, or a marked rhythmic/metrical pattern in its wording, independent of any title pun; score 0 if the wording has no notable sonic patterning.
selected.rationale: R60 ('Meth'd up Mondays', alliteration/rhyme echoing 'Manic Monday', dense .860/card .299), R42 ('Up the Holler', rhythmic phrase, dense .961/card .363), and R33 ('barbecue flavored beard', alliterative, dense .260/card .762) show sonic wordplay recurring on both sides of the disagreement.
member_names: Asyndetic noun-list cadence for comic rhythm

selected.name: Title Reengineering Depth
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable title is transformed into a coherent, substantive new premise; score 0 when the change is merely a superficial name swap.
selected.rationale: R06 and R19 turn familiar movie titles into specific political premises, unlike thinner title substitutions such as R28 and R35.

selected.name: Joke mechanism matches the hashtag's named genre
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the specific comedic technique used (e.g. genuine fright/unease for a 'scary story' tag, a plausible-sounding title for a 'movies' tag) is exactly what the contest's named theme calls for, such that the joke would lose its point if pasted into a different hashtag's contest; score 0 if the tweet's content is generic and could be pasted under an unrelated contest hashtag with no loss of sense or effect.
selected.rationale: Within the same #Scary_Story_In_5_Words tag, R56 ('Mother visits me, stays FOREVER', genuinely unsettling, dense .966/card .407) is dense-favored while R25 ('Cubs Win the World Series ... #STLCards', a sports non-sequitur with no fright content, dense .029/card .775) and R48 ('Star Wars VII: series finale', a movie pun with no scary content, dense .135/card .980) are card-favored despite delivering none of the named genre's actual mechanism.
member_names: Joke mechanism matches the hashtag's named genre

selected.name: List whose final item swerves against the earlier ones
selected.instruction: For entries built as a list or triple, score whether the last item breaks the pattern the earlier items set, retroactively reframing them. 10 = the first items establish a comfortable category and the final item lands in a different register, turning the list into an argument. 5 = a list with a rhythmically satisfying but categorically flat close. 0 = an undifferentiated inventory in which the items are interchangeable and the order does not matter. Entries that are not lists should be scored on whether their final word similarly redirects what came before.
selected.rationale: R45 'Guns Nascar Beer Oligarchy' sets up three tailgate nouns and closes with a political indictment; R29 'Guns, No Abortions' sets a pairing that turns on the reader. Both sit dense-high with low card scores (0.699/0.194 and 0.848/0.159). By contrast R34 'Corn syrup and salt' and R49-style flat inventories are interchangeable lists. A bank with a wordplay or list-structure item scores the surface form, not whether the last slot does work.
member_names: List whose final item swerves against the earlier ones

selected.name: Consistent in-character dialect/persona voice
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the entire tweet is phrased as a first-person or address-form line in a sustained, distinct social voice/dialect appropriate to the contest's target persona; score 5 if a persona voice is present but inconsistent or thin; score 0 if the tweet is written in neutral, voiceless description with no persona.
selected.rationale: R24 ('I Speak 'Merican!', dense .929/card .365), R42 ('Up the Holler', dense .961/card .363), and R52 ('Tell you what.', dense .740/card .257) are persona-voiced lines the dense model consistently ranks high relative to the scorecard.

selected.name: Stereotype Avoidance
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the entry approaches the theme through an unusual, non-interchangeable detail; score 0 when it is an expected stereotype bundle that could fit almost any entry.
selected.rationale: R14 and R34 use familiar redneck shorthand, making them useful contrasts for judging freshness beyond topical fit.

selected.name: Pun stacks two or more meanings at once
selected.instruction: Score 10 if the tweet's central wordplay simultaneously activates two distinct meanings or reference registers at once (e.g. a title pun that ALSO carries a separate topical/political meaning); score 5 if there is a pun but only a single register of meaning; score 0 if there is no pun or double meaning present.
selected.rationale: R20 ('Kill Bill of Rights' stacks a movie-title pun with a constitutional register) and R55 ('What Ever Happened to Baby Jane's Healthcare?' stacks a movie-title pun with a healthcare-policy jab) both stack two registers, as does R28 ('Proud Republican Tools', stacking literal and idiomatic senses of 'tools'); these appear on both sides of the disagreement, marking double-stacking as a distinct axis worth isolating from single-register puns.
member_names: Pun stacks two or more meanings at once

selected.name: Spoken in character versus described from outside
selected.instruction: Score how far the entry is an utterance a person from the prompt's world would actually say, rather than a third-party description of such a person. 10 = the line is pure in-character speech, with the speaker's own diction, deixis and attitude carried by the words themselves (a quoted brag, threat, complaint, or aside that presupposes a whole speaker). 5 = a noun phrase with some voiced coloring but no clear speaker. 0 = a flat outside-observer label or field-note about the type, with no one speaking, e.g. a bare descriptive noun phrase an anthropologist could have written. Judge only from the wording: presence of second person, contractions, dialect spelling, interjections and vocatives raise the score; bare nominal inventories lower it. Do not reward mere rudeness.
selected.rationale: The dense-favored side of the slice is dominated by lines that are said, not observed: R56 'Y'all watch this', R60 'Tell you what.', R17 'That's my uncledad!', R10 'I Speak Merican!'. The scorecard-favored side is dominated by outside descriptions of the same stereotype: R37 'Toothless mug shot', R36 'barbecue flavored beard', R25 'WalMart special occasion'. A bank scoring topical fit and stereotype relevance would rate those descriptions equally well while missing that no one is talking.
member_names: Spoken in character versus described from outside

selected.name: Reliance on franchise scaffolding: sequel numbers, colons, subtitles
selected.instruction: Score inversely to how much of the construction is carried by borrowed title furniture. 0-3 = the entry leans on sequel numerals, colons, subtitles, or roman numerals to hold the joke together, so the structure comes pre-supplied by the source and the contributed content is a single grafted word or phrase. 5 = one such device used but the contributed material carries the line. 10 = no borrowed scaffolding; the entry stands as a complete phrase whose shape the writer chose. Judge the presence and load-bearing role of the furniture, not the topic.
selected.rationale: The scaffolding-heavy rows cluster on the scorecard-high side: R53 'Speed 2: Control Ted Cruz', R47 'Carbon Emission Impossible 3: Coal Nation', R52 'Star Wars VII: series finale', R48 '12 Angry Men : The Contenders'. None of the dense-favored rows uses a sequel number or subtitle colon in this way. A criterion bank rewarding recognizable-title usage and structural completeness will score the furniture itself, treating a colon as evidence of craft.
member_names: Reliance on franchise scaffolding: sequel numbers, colons, subtitles

selected.name: Extra hashtags beyond the contest tag
selected.instruction: Score the extent of hashtag material that is not the contest hashtag. 10 = two or more additional hashtags are present, including tags that address a fan community, a sports allegiance, a personal occasion, or the contest's own scoring culture. 5 = exactly one additional hashtag. 0 = only the contest hashtag appears. Count tags; do not assess whether they are relevant, witty, or annoying, and do not let the joke's content affect the score.
selected.rationale: R01 carries '#PointsMe #July4thBirthday' alongside the contest tag and sits at dense 0.042 with card 0.542; R53 carries '#STLCards' and sits at dense 0.223 with card 0.926. In both cases the extra tags do no comic work at all: they address people outside the contest. The conjectured parent (an author seeking amplification or speaking to a private circle) has no plausible path to making the entry itself funnier, so I tag it unmixed.
member_names: Administrative prefix versus trailing signature placement of handle and hashtag
Extra hashtags beyond the contest tag
Extra hashtags or links beyond the single contest tag
Handle/hashtag block placed before vs after the joke text

selected.name: Partisan-trigger density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text contains explicit partisan, ideological, or politically polarizing cues; judge cue intensity only, not whether the entry is good.
selected.rationale: Political identity cues can attract or repel audiences for reasons unrelated to the line's craft. Visible examples include R11, R18, R41, R53, and R58.

selected.name: Temporal anchoring
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of explicit years, numbered installments, current-event references, or time-sensitive cultural anchors; judge only temporal specificity, not whether the reference is timely or good.
selected.rationale: When an item is written relative to a news or cultural cycle, the timing may leave dated-reference fingerprints that models exploit independently of quality. R29 specifies 2013, R30 invokes the Cubs winning the World Series, and R10 names Star Wars VII.
selected.upstream_parent: submission timing and topical news cycle
upstream_parent_all_members: submission timing and topical news cycle

selected.name: Presence of an attached URL or media pointer
selected.instruction: Score how much of the item consists of, or points to, material outside the text. 10 = the item carries a t.co or other URL, or otherwise explicitly refers the reader to an attached picture, video or linked page. 5 = a quoted or reported fragment implying an external source but with no link present. 0 = plain text with no link and no pointer. Score only the presence and prominence of the pointer. Do not attempt to judge whether the link helps or hurts the entry, and do not speculate about what is on the other end.
selected.rationale: The three link-bearing rows are the three lowest dense percentiles in the entire 60-row slice, and all three sit mid-to-high on the card: R50 'automotive lawn art http://t.co/...' (0.010/0.804), R35 'David Brent in porn flick ... https://t.co/...' (0.022/0.591), R26 'I saw myself on @midnight ... https://t.co/...' (0.049/0.554). A model can key on the literal 't.co' string without any understanding of the joke, which makes this a textual fingerprint of how the tweet was composed rather than of what it says. I tag mixed because the same parent (the joke actually living in an attached image) can plausibly also mean the visible text really is a weaker standalone entry.
member_names: Presence of an attached URL or media pointer
selected.upstream_parent: composition mode: the entry was authored as a photo or link tweet from a client that appends a URL
upstream_parent_all_members: composition mode: the entry was authored as a photo or link tweet from a client that appends a URL

selected.name: Stock phrase reuse
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the wording resembles a familiar slogan, catchphrase, idiom, or reusable template; judge only recognizability and reuse, not whether the phrase is effective.
selected.rationale: Highly familiar phrasing supplies a memorability or corpus-frequency shortcut unrelated to intrinsic contest quality. R20 echoes a song phrase, R43 uses Gee, Thanks Obama, and R47 uses a commercial slogan.
upstream_parent_all_members: author's reuse of culturally circulating templates

selected.name: Proper-noun reference density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the tweet uses named people, franchises, films, institutions, or other recognizable entities; judge only reference density, not whether the references are effective.
selected.rationale: A writer's repertoire and presumed audience can produce recognizable-reference fingerprints that models may use as shortcuts, while repertoire can also affect genuine writing ability. R04 names Jar Jar Binks, R16 names Bradley Cooper, and R17 invokes a film title.
selected.upstream_parent: author's media repertoire and audience familiarity
upstream_parent_all_members: audience familiarity and shared cultural knowledge
author's media repertoire and audience familiarity

selected.name: Reference predictability / top-of-mind obviousness within its category
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how likely it is that many different people, independently and without seeing each other's answers, would land on the exact same reference the tweet uses (i.e. how canonical/first-guess the referenced title, phrase, or figure is for this prompt category): 0 = an obscure or highly idiosyncratic reference unlikely to be duplicated; 10 = the single most obvious, textbook reference for the category, of the kind many entrants would independently reach for. Score only this predictability, never whether the joke built on it is good.
selected.rationale: R41 ('12 Angry Men : The Contenders') and R28 ('16 Angry Men (and one woman)') independently riff on the identical famous title, as do R38 ('Jar Jar Binks spin-off movie') and R08 ('Star Wars 7 With JarJar') on Star Wars/Jar Jar -- these duplications show the reference pool has crowded, highly-predictable landing spots; an item's position in the submission stream (how early/obvious a take it is) can leave this kind of trace without being a direct read on the entry's own craft.
member_names: Reference predictability / top-of-mind obviousness within its category
selected.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream / idea-crowding (obvious ideas get submitted first and are independently duplicated by many entrants, which can affect how fresh or stale a reader/judge perceives an entry as)
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream / idea-crowding (obvious ideas get submitted first and are independently duplicated by many entrants, which can affect how fresh or stale a reader/judge perceives an entry as)

selected.name: Obvious-first-take fingerprint
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how strongly the text reads as a default, immediately available association to the prompt, using familiar topical ingredients or a conventional premise; judge only those first-association cues, not originality or quality.
selected.rationale: Early or crowded submission positions can encourage default prompt associations, leaving a textual trace even when actual position is unseen. R25 lists conventional redneck symbols, while R34 and R50 use direct, familiar prompt associations.
selected.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream or submission timing
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream or submission timing

selected.name: Taboo-trigger density
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much the text invokes sex, drugs, bodily functions, violence, death, or other taboo material; judge taboo presence only, not whether the entry is good.
selected.rationale: Taboo cues can change audience reaction or distribution independently of comic quality. They are visible in R12, R39, R50, and R51.

upstream_parent_all_members: audience norm sensitivity and platform-moderation climate

selected.name: Contest boilerplate load
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for how much of the text consists of contest/platform boilerplate such as @midnight, the contest hashtag, or their repeated placement; judge visible boilerplate only, not whether the entry is good.
selected.rationale: Submission-format habits can predict how an item is processed without describing its comic construction. Compare the packaging patterns in R01, R03, R08, and R47.
